items.title: Inteligencia artificial en psiquiatría: usos y promesas
items.abstract: This article examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry, highlighting both its transformative potential and its ethical, clinical, and philosophical challenges. AI applications (ranging from diagnostic algorithms and predictive models to therapeutic chatbots and neuroimplants) are reshaping mental healthcare by improving early detection, personalizing treatments, and expanding access to services, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced techniques such as machine learning and natural language processing enable the analysis of multimodal data, enhancing clinical decision-making and enabling preventive interventions. However, the adoption of AI raises significant concerns. These include risks to privacy, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, and challenges in ensuring informed consent, particularly in vulnerable psychiatric populations. Neurotechnologies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when assisted by AI, introduce further ethical dilemmas related to autonomy, identity, and long-term safety. The article argues that these challenges cannot be addressed without a deeper conceptual understanding of mental disorders. It advocates for a pluralistic and enactivist framework, which views mental health conditions as dynamic interactions between brain, body, and environment. Ultimately, the responsible integration of AI in psychiatry requires robust ethical governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a human-centered approach.

items.title: Interdisciplinary Case Design and Exploration for Machine Learning Course
items.abstract: Traditional machine learning teaching commonly suffers from repetitive experimental paradigms and narrow real-world application contexts, which leads students to rely on mechanical code replication and surface-level learning. This instructional pattern fails to cultivate interdisciplinary cognition and humanistic accomplishment. To improve the current teaching deficiencies, this study adopts digitized Dunhuang mural resources as an innovative teaching medium to develop interdisciplinary practice cases. Following the design concepts of staged ability progression, integration of technical and artistic perspectives, and authentic scenario orientation, this research constructs a three-tier teaching system including basic training, in-depth exploration and comprehensive innovation. The practical curriculum covers a full range of computer vision tasks: Dunhuang image preprocessing, stylistic discrimination, CNN visual recognition, artistic style migration, decorative pattern generation, and damaged mural inpainting. All experimental units combine algorithm engineering practice with Dunhuang art and cultural instruction. This study develops two-dimensional teaching support resources. It also constructs a tailored T-A-P evaluation system that integrates technical ability, artistic attainment and practical performance. The comprehensive student assessment covers coding skills, model error analysis and cultural aesthetic understanding. Classroom teaching practice has proven that the designed case system can significantly strengthen students’ machine learning engineering capabilities and enrich their cultural accomplishment. This research offers a feasible and referable paradigm for interdisciplinary integration in artificial intelligence teaching.

items.title: INTERNALISASI NILAI-NILAI AKHLAK DALAM PEMBELAJARAN PAI DI ERA ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UNTUK MEMBENTUK ETIKA PESERTA DIDIK
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education presents both opportunities and challenges for shaping students’ ethical behavior. This study aims to analyze the internalization of moral values in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) as a foundation for developing students’ ethical behavior in the use of AI. Theoretically, this study contributes to the development of Islamic Religious Education and moral education scholarship in responding to technological advancement, while practically providing a foundation for developing AI-oriented ethical learning in PAI. This study employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and documentation and analyzed thematically through coding, categorization, theme identification, and interpretation. The findings indicate that the internalization of moral values occurs through several interconnected stages: value recognition, critical understanding, appreciation, habituation, and actualization. The values of ṣidq (honesty), amanah (trustworthiness), responsibility, tabayyun (verification), respect for others’ work, and self-control constitute important foundations for shaping students’ ethical behavior when using AI. The novelty of this study lies in proposing an akhlaq-based AI literacy perspective, integrating technological literacy with the internalization of Islamic moral values in PAI learning. This perspective positions AI not merely as a learning technology but also as a new context for character formation and ethical development among students.

items.title: Internet search use is more strongly associated with low cognitive function than digital device ownership among community-dwelling older adults
items.abstract: Digital device use has been associated with cognitive function; however, device ownership and internet search use are often considered together despite potentially differing levels of cognitive engagement. To examine the associations of digital device ownership and internet search use with low cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults. This cross-sectional study included 821 community-dwelling older adults (mean age, 78.4 ± 5.7 years; 91.7% female). Digital device ownership and internet search use were assessed by self-report. Participants were categorized as non-digital device owners, device owners without internet search use, or device owners with internet search use. Cognitive function was assessed using a validated virtual reality-based eye-tracking examination, and low cognitive function was defined as a total score below 75. Logistic regression analyses examined the associations between group membership and low cognitive function after adjustment for age, sex, educational level, living status, polypharmacy, depressive symptoms, hypertension, history of stroke, and history of Parkinson’s disease. The prevalence of low cognitive function was 70.2% among non-digital device owners, 57.8% among device owners without internet search use, and 30.6% among device owners with internet search use. Compared with non-digital device owners, device owners without internet search use did not have significantly different odds of low cognitive function (odds ratio: 0.70; 95% confidence interval: 0.37–1.35; P = .291), whereas device owners with internet search use had significantly lower odds (odds ratio: 0.39; 95% confidence interval: 0.20–0.75; P = .005). Digital device ownership accompanied by internet search use was more strongly associated with lower odds of low cognitive function than ownership alone.

items.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Narrative Framing Classification: A TF-IDF-Based Study of Frankenstein
items.abstract: This study evaluates interpretable supervised machine learning for three-class narrative framing classification of literary text, using Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) as a case study; narrative framing is the evaluative position a passage assigns to the Creature: Threat, Victim, or Ambivalent. The methodology comprised five stages: (1) extraction of passages narrated by Victor Frankenstein, the Creature, and Robert Walton from the 1818 Project Gutenberg text; (2) annotation of 195 passages, with a blinded second annotator re-labeling 68 passages (Cohen's κ = 0.6926); (3) sublinear TF-IDF unigram and bigram representation; (4) classification with Multinomial Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, and Logistic Regression against Majority and VADER baselines under stratified 5-fold cross-validation; and (5) a designation-masking ablation and coefficient analysis. The results show that Logistic Regression obtained the highest mean scores (66.67% accuracy; 47.75% Macro-F1), although its margin over Linear SVM (46.18%) and VADER (44.85%) lies within fold-level variability. Pooled F1 reached 69.0% for Threat and 74.3% for Victim, whereas none of the 29 Ambivalent passages was correctly identified. Masking explicit designations reduced Macro-F1 only to 45.20%, indicating partial robustness to this procedure rather than discourse-level modeling. It is concluded that interpretable classical classifiers can separate Threat from Victim framing using transparent lexical evidence but cannot yet detect ambiguous framing; given the single-novel, small, and imbalanced dataset, the findings are a preliminary proof of concept. Future work should enlarge and balance the corpus, apply group-based and repeated cross-validation, and compare context-aware models, including large language models, on the Ambivalent class.

items.title: Intersecting families with large covering number - On a conjecture of Frankl, Ota, and Tokushige
items.abstract: Stability theorems on intersecting families are often formulated via the covering number of set families. Let $M(n,k,t)$ denote the maximum size of a $k$-uniform intersecting family $\mathcal F\subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}$ with covering number $t$. It is known that for any fixed $t$ and fixed $k$ sufficiently large relative to $t$, one has $M(n,k,t)=(p_{t-1}(k)+o(1))(k)\binom{n}{k}$ as $n$ tends to infinity, where $p_{t-1}(k)$ is the maximum number of covers of size $t-1$ that a $k$-uniform intersecting family can have provided its covering number is $t-1$. Frankl, Ota, and Tokushige conjectured that $p_t(k)=k^t-\binom{t}{2}k^{t-1}+O_t(k^{t-2})$ for fixed $t$ as $k$ tends to infinity and they also showed that $p_t(k)=k^t-b(t)k^{t-1}+O_t(k^{t-2})$, where $b(t)$ is defined as the extremum of the following minimization problem. Suppose a $k$-uniform intersecting family $\mathcal F$ of covering number $t$ can be partitioned into $\mathcal F_1,\dots,\mathcal F_t$ such that for every $i$ there exists a set $X_i$ with $X_i \subseteq F_i$ for all $F_i\in\mathcal F_i$ and the $X_i$'s are pairwise disjoint and non-empty. Then $b(t)$ is the minimum of $\sum_{i=1}^t(k-|X_i|)$ over all such families, partitions and $X_i$'s. In accordance with the conjecture on $p_t(k)$, Frankl, Ota, and Tokushige conjectured $b(t)=\binom{t}{2}$ for all $t\ge 2$ and proved $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lfloor \frac{t-1}{2}\rfloor^{3/2}\le b(t)\le \binom{t}{2}$. In this note, we present a counterexample to the conjecture showing $b(t)\le 2\sqrt2\,t^{3/2}\sqrt{\log t}$ $+O(t^{3/2})$ and improve the lower bound to $\frac{2}{3^{3/4}}t^{3/2}-O(t)\le b(t)$. The counterexample was found by ChatGPT 6.1Sol, the lower bound proof is due to the human author.

items.title: InterWebCoder: Learning Interactive Webpage Generation from Executable Tests via Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Interactive webpages underpin modern applications, but reproducing both their visual appearance and multi-step behavior remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Scalable training data must capture user actions, state transitions, and expected outcomes, while real-world webpage code is often entangled with irrelevant scripts and external dependencies. Moreover, existing GUI-agent-based verification provides slow and potentially unstable functional feedback. To address these challenges, we propose InterWebCoder, an efficient framework for interactive webpage code generation. InterWebCoder introduces a Test-Specification-Guided and Execution-Verified Data Synthesis pipeline that records real-world interaction trajectories and synthesizes self-contained webpage code with executable test scripts. A failureattributed repair mechanism uses runtime evidence to locate and iteratively fix errors in either the webpage code or test script. We then combine test-ID-weighted supervised fine-tuning with group-relative policy optimization, directly optimizing functional correctness and visual fidelity using test pass rates and state-level visual similarity. This replaces costly GUI-agent verification with fast, reproducible executable feedback. Our pipeline produces 1,736 verified samples from 2,058 tasks, achieving an 84.35% synthesis success rate. On IWR-Bench and Vision2Web, InterWebCoder achieves final scores of 48.54 and 48.42 with a 9B backbone, outperforming 30B-level models and Gemini-3.7-Flash while remaining competitive with Claude-Sonnet-5. It reduces reward-computation latency by over 97%, eliminates external MLLM verification costs, and accelerates end-to-end training by up to 1.4x.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: Abstract This introductory chapter has three sections. Section 1.1, begins by explaining the concept of welfare. In short, AIs have welfare just in case they are worthy of a certain distinctive kind of moral consideration. Then, it surveys the leading theories of welfare, which claim that welfare consists in pleasure, or satisfied desire, or participation in what is objectively good. It argues that these theories agree that whether AIs have welfare depends on three factors: agency, consciousness, and sentience. Section 1.2 reflects on methodology. The arguments in subsequent chapters presuppose functionalism, which understands mental states in terms of complex patterns of causation. The book also adopts a top-down methodology, which applies existing philosophical theories of agency, consciousness, and sentience to AIs. Section 1.3 introduces the AIs discussed in the book: large language models, language model agents, and reinforcement learners.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: This chapter introduces artificial intelligence as an economic phenomenon rather than as a purely technical achievement. It defines AI, in the language of economics, as a family of technologies that lowers the cost of prediction, pattern recognition, classification, content generation, and increasingly decision support. The chapter explains why this cost shock matters for productivity, labor demand, inequality, market structure, state capacity, and global development. It also situates AI within the longer history of general-purpose technologies such as steam, electricity, and information technology, while emphasizing the distinctive feature of contemporary AI: its ability to enter non-routine cognitive tasks previously protected from automation. The chapter presents the organizing framework of the book. AI does not simply “replace jobs” or “create growth”. It reallocates tasks, changes complementarities between humans and capital, alters firm boundaries, and forces governments to rethink taxation, regulation, education, and social insurance. The chapter concludes with a roadmap for the remaining chapters.

items.title: Introduction to the Concept of AI in Sports Science
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the concept of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science and situates it within the broader transformation of sport into a data-driven and analytically intensive domain. It argues that Artificial Intelligence has evolved from a supportive computational tool into an active component of decision-making processes in performance optimization, injury prevention, training design, and sport management. The chapter traces the historical and conceptual origins of Artificial Intelligence, from early philosophical reflections and mechanical prototypes to the emergence of modern data-intensive systems enabled by advances in computational power and large-scale data availability. Building on this context, the chapter establishes sport as an ideal empirical environment for AI applications due to its structured rules, measurable outcomes, and continuous data generation. It introduces key methodological paradigms, particularly supervised learning and unsupervised learning, and explains their complementary roles in predictive modeling and pattern discovery within sports analytics. By integrating historical perspective, conceptual clarification, and methodological foundations, this chapter provides a structured entry point into machine learning, data-driven analysis, and performance modelling in sport, forming the theoretical basis for subsequent chapters focused on neural networks, Bayesian inference, and advanced AI applications in Sports Science.

items.title: INTUITION AND MECHANISMS OF ITS KNOWLEDGE IN THE CONTEXT OF MODERN CYBERNETICS AND THE THEORY OF COMPLEX SYSTEMS
items.abstract: This article presents the fundamental foundations and specific characteristics of intuition, as well as the mechanisms for its comprehension, particularly within the framework of cybernetics and complex systems theory. Today, intuition is understood in science as a multi-level and complex phenomenon, the process of cognition of which includes both rational and irrational components. The authors convincingly argue that intuition has its own structure and a certain logic; it can be considered within the framework of nonlinear dynamics as a self-organizing system with feedback and multiple mechanisms. The analysis shows that intuitive knowledge arises where research encounters high rates of change not only in the environment but also in its component parts, incomplete empirical data, and a lack of resources. As is well known, the concept of “observer” is introduced within the paradigm of post-non-classical science, particularly within the context of the evolutionary-constructive model of scientific knowledge development. Now the observer is directly viewed as part of the system, and their intuitive decisions are perceived as the result of the interaction of internal cognitive structures with external information flows. As a result, it becomes possible to interpret intuition as a significant factor in cognition, capable of minimizing the tacitness and uncertainty of knowledge. Thus, intuition becomes a natural and objective regulator of the formation of new knowledge through the synthesis of heterogeneous information. Intuition and its mechanisms are well suited to the theory of complex systems. In particular, the phenomenon of self-organization, especially emergence in intuition, is a nonlinear interaction between system elements, resulting in transitions between different cognitive states and the formation of qualitatively new types of knowledge. Research demonstrates how and by what means parallels arise between human intuition and constructed models, how weak and implicit signals are recognized, and how intuitive probabilistic predictions are formed. Conclusion: Intuition is a unique phenomenon, a special adaptive mechanism for knowledge processing, essential for the successful functioning of humans and intelligent systems in the context of the nonequilibrium of the modern world and the increasing complexity of cognitive processes, encompassing both physical reality and the metaphysics of existence. This approach offers new prospects for the development of hybrid human-machine systems, where intuitive and rational mechanisms interact as complementary modes of cognition.

items.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
items.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

items.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study
items.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

items.abstract: The Physical Limit of Capital: Energy, Infrastructure and Geopolitics in the New Resource Economy ISHEA Premiere Report · Vol. 1, No. 1 · September 2026 This report examines the relationship between financial capital, physical resource availability, infrastructure resilience, and geopolitical risk in the global economy. It explores how the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, the reconfiguration of energy and mineral supply chains, and the strategic transformation of maritime and logistics corridors are reshaping the conditions under which financial value can be converted into realizable economic activity. Using an interdisciplinary analytical framework informed by biophysical accounting, bioenergetics, cognitive economics, complex systems, and resilience analysis, the report examines three interconnected dimensions: the physical infrastructure supporting AI-related investment; the strategic role of energy resources and logistics corridors in international capital allocation; and the implications of geopolitical disruption for asset valuation and business planning. The report introduces an ISHEA analytical heuristic, Realizable Value, which considers financial value alongside physical availability, logistical resilience, and flow security. This formulation is presented as a diagnostic framework rather than a calibrated or empirically validated valuation model. The report concludes with practical recommendations for business planning in 2026–2027, including physical-dependency audits, geographic and supplier redundancy, energy-risk assessment, and systemic stress testing. Purpose: To contribute to interdisciplinary discussion on the relationship between financial valuation and the physical, infrastructural, and geopolitical conditions that sustain economic activity. items.title: Judging Reliability and Technology-Assisted Performance Evaluation in DanceSport and Other Judged Sports: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: FAIR-DANCE is a scoping review of judging reliability, scoring validity, contextual effects, judge performance, and technology-assisted performance evaluation in DanceSport and other judged sports. This OSF project hosts the review protocol, search documentation, screening and retrieval records, final data-charting dataset, supplementary materials, reporting checklists, methodological amendments, and reproducibility materials. The review maps evidence on reliability and agreement, scoring accuracy and validity, contextual bias, anomalous scoring behaviour, judge education and calibration, competition monitoring and evaluation procedures, digital systems, statistical analytics, and artificial intelligence-supported assessment, with particular emphasis on the potential transferability of these approaches to DanceSport. The review was conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute methodological guidance for scoping reviews and is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Original searches were conducted in Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and PubMed/MEDLINE. A targeted supplementary Scopus sensitivity search conducted on 6 October 2026 identified 10 additional eligible studies, yielding a final analytic corpus of 123 studies. The final synthesis is organised around five complementary dimensions: Measurement Quality, Contextual Fairness, Scoring Monitoring and Anomaly Detection, Technology-Assisted Evaluation, and Evaluation Procedures and Feedback. Continuous judge education and calibration and human-in-the-loop technology are treated as cross-cutting mechanisms supporting technical performance evaluation. Post-registration methodological amendments, supplementary-search decisions, and the complete reproducibility audit trail are documented transparently in this project.

items.title: Kecerdasan Buatan Dalam Transformasi Interpretasi Radiologi: Sebuah Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis
items.abstract: Latar belakang: Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) telah mengubah paradigma interpretasi gambar radiologi secara fundamental. Kemampuan deep learning dan machine learning membuka peluang peningkatan akurasi diagnostik, efisiensi waktu pembacaan, dan pengurangan variabilitas antar-pembaca. Namun, bukti komprehensif mengenai dampak AI terhadap berbagai modalitas pencitraan medis masih perlu disintesis secara sistematis. Tujuan: Melakukan tinjauan literatur sistematis (SLR) untuk mensintesis bukti ilmiah mengenai dampak AI terhadap akurasi diagnostik, waktu interpretasi, kepercayaan diagnostik, dan faktor-faktor yang memengaruhi interaksi manusia-AI dalam interpretasi radiologi. Metode: Penelitian ini menggunakan metode SLR mengacu pada panduan PRISMA 2020. Pencarian dilakukan pada PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, dan IEEE Xplore (2021–2025). Dari 847 artikel teridentifikasi, 9 memenuhi kriteria inklusi. Hasil: Sembilan studi mencakup mamografi, rontgen dada, CT scan, MRI, angiografi, dan radiografi muskuloskeletal dengan lebih dari 100.000 kasus. AI meningkatkan sensitivitas diagnostik rata-rata 11,4–23,0%, memperpendek waktu pembacaan kasus normal (rerata 13,3 vs 14,8 detik), dan meningkatkan kepercayaan diagnostik. Kesimpulan: AI terbukti konsisten meningkatkan performa diagnostik radiologi tanpa mengurangi produktivitas.

items.title: Kelas Kreatif AI Canva Untuk Siswa Program PkM di SMAN 1 Lebak Wangi
items.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi digital dan kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) telah membuka peluang baru dalam dunia pendidikan, khususnya dalam pengembangan kreativitas dan literasi digital peserta didik. Namun, masih banyak siswa yang belum mampu memanfaatkan teknologi desain digital secara optimal untuk mendukung kegiatan pembelajaran dan pengabdian kepada masyarakat. Oleh karena itu, kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (PkM) ini bertujuan meningkatkan pemahaman, keterampilan, dan kesiapan siswa dalam menggunakan aplikasi Canva berbasis AI melalui program Pelatihan Kelas Kreatif AI Canva bagi siswa PKM SMAN 1 Lebak Wangi. Metode pelaksanaan kegiatan meliputi ceramah, demonstrasi, praktik langsung (learning by doing), diskusi, pendampingan, dan evaluasi. Keberhasilan program diukur melalui beberapa indikator, yaitu pemahaman materi, kemudahan penggunaan Canva, proses pembuatan desain, kualitas konten, pembelajaran, kolaborasi, fasilitasi, etika dan literasi digital, serta niat menggunakan Canva. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa pelatihan memberikan dampak positif yang signifikan dengan rata-rata capaian sebesar 81,4%, melampaui target yang ditetapkan sebesar 75%. Peningkatan tertinggi terjadi pada indikator kemudahan penggunaan Canva dan niat menggunakan Canva yang masing-masing mencapai 100%, menunjukkan tingginya penerimaan dan motivasi siswa dalam memanfaatkan teknologi AI. Selain itu, peserta berhasil menghasilkan berbagai karya digital berupa poster, infografis, dan media presentasi yang kreatif serta komunikatif. Kegiatan ini membuktikan bahwa pelatihan Canva berbasis AI efektif dalam meningkatkan literasi digital, kreativitas, dan keterampilan desain visual siswa. Program ini juga berkontribusi dalam mempersiapkan generasi muda yang adaptif, inovatif, dan siap menghadapi tantangan transformasi digital di era Society 5.0.

items.abstract: WHEN A CIVILIZATION NO LONGER KNOWS WHERE TO PLACE ITS PEOPLE A BIT Essay on Education, Work, Human Value, and the Finite Human Life Cycle Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This interdisciplinary social and philosophical essay examines a growing concern in modern civilization: the potential disconnection between human educational achievement, accumulated capabilities, labor-market structures, and meaningful participation in society. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay begins with a reported case of a highly educated individual experiencing prolonged difficulty entering stable employment. Rather than interpreting an individual case as evidence of universal labor-market failure, the essay investigates the structural interfaces between education, professional training, recruitment, technological change, and the finite human life cycle. A central argument is that education, businesses, technological systems, and public institutions often operate on different timescales. Education may require many years. Recruitment decisions may be made within months. Technologies can transform occupations rapidly, while human lives continue through irreversible biological and social stages. When these systems become misaligned, the costs of institutional mismatch may be transferred disproportionately to individuals. The essay introduces a BIT interpretation of historical outcomes (Quả lịch sử), emphasizing that a person's abilities and achievements represent accumulated life histories rather than isolated qualifications or current employment status. It discusses the compression of human capabilities into résumés, the disappearance of entry-level opportunities, unused professional knowledge, and the potential loss of social participation when qualified individuals cannot find meaningful opportunities to contribute. The essay proposes examining the transition between education and employment as an important form of social infrastructure. Possible responses include professional transition pathways, mentorship, supervised work opportunities, recognition of transferable capabilities, and institutions capable of connecting human knowledge with real societal needs. Central Proposition A civilization should not be evaluated only by how many people it educates, but also by its ability to transform their accumulated knowledge and capabilities into meaningful participation in collective life. Scope and Limitations This publication is a social and philosophical thought essay, not an empirical demonstration that higher education has lost its value or that artificial intelligence is the cause of unemployment. It does not treat a single reported employment case as representative of the entire labor market. Its purpose is to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about education, employment, human dignity, institutional responsibility, and the preservation of human potential throughout finite life cycles. The original Vietnamese essay references reporting from The Wall Street Journal and materials from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the National Science Foundation's National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. items.abstract: When the Collective Foundation Changes Rhythm A Conditional Foresight Essay on Children, Digital Environments, and the New Historical Outcomes of Humanity Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores how changes in modern environments may influence the formation, transmission, and transformation of collective behavioral foundations across generations. Developed from Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Source Ontology Framework 03, the essay examines the relationship between intrinsic human characteristics, historical collective foundations, environmental change, and emerging technological systems. The central question concerns what may happen when the environments shaping human development change much faster than the biological and structural characteristics of human beings. The essay explores nine conditional future perspectives, including: The increasing difference between long-term intrinsic human characteristics and rapidly changing environments. Digital screens and online interactions becoming major channels through which children acquire and retain experiences. Changes in the relative influence of families, schools, digital platforms, and artificial intelligence on childhood development. Individuals participating simultaneously in multiple overlapping historical and cultural collective foundations. Artificial intelligence becoming an active component in cycles of information retention, behavioral feedback, and social interaction. The growing difficulty of separating intrinsic tendencies from environmentally acquired behavior. Educational approaches moving beyond immediate measurable outcomes toward the design of developmental environments. Societies recognizing how their institutions, technologies, and daily practices shape the foundations inherited by future generations. The possibility of multiple future developmental trajectories rather than one predetermined collective destiny. The BIT cycle Tính – Lưu – Hành – Quả – Tính serves as a conceptual framework for considering how environmental interactions become retained patterns and how present outcomes influence subsequent generations. A central idea is that every generation inherits not only an existing world but also historically established rhythms, practices, expectations, and systems of interaction. Through its activities, each generation may preserve, transform, or replace parts of these inherited foundations. The essay does not assume that digital technology is universally beneficial or harmful. Its potential effects depend on technological design, family environments, education, communities, institutions, and the specific histories of different societies. Scientific scope and limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an experimentally validated theory of human development. It does not predict that collective human behavior must follow a single technological, social, or historical trajectory. The proposed perspectives are intended to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about childhood, education, technological environments, human adaptability, artificial intelligence, and responsibility toward future generations. items.abstract: WHEN A DEGREE IS NO LONGER A PROMISE A Conditional Foresight Essay on Education, Employment, and Human Life-Cycle Transition Infrastructure Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores possible transformations in education, employment, professional identity, and social institutions as artificial intelligence, automation, and rapidly changing economic structures reshape the relationship between human knowledge and work. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay asks whether future civilization will be able to maintain meaningful transitions between learning, professional contribution, personal development, and a dignified human life. The essay presents nine conditional future perspectives. First, academic degrees may increasingly function as evidence of educational achievement rather than implicit guarantees of specific professional positions. Second, automation and artificial intelligence may reduce certain entry-level tasks, potentially weakening traditional pathways through which younger generations acquire professional experience. Third, institutions may develop transferable capability profiles that recognize practical skills, interdisciplinary competence, and demonstrated problem-solving ability beyond conventional occupational titles. Fourth, universities may expand their responsibilities by supporting graduates through longer professional transitions rather than ending institutional support at graduation. Fifth, countries may begin treating unused human expertise as a potential public resource, creating mechanisms to connect available capabilities with unmet social needs. Sixth, careers may increasingly involve multiple transitions among employment, education, independent work, care responsibilities, and periods of recovery. Seventh, artificial intelligence may improve labor-market matching while simultaneously creating new risks of algorithmic exclusion, opacity, and unfair screening. Eighth, future institutions may recognize periods of unemployment, retraining, caregiving, and independent research as legitimate phases of human development rather than treating them as personal deficiencies. Ninth, the evaluation of education and employment policies may shift toward their long-term effects on the complete human life cycle, including health, family formation, professional resilience, social participation, and security in later life. Central Proposition The future value of education may depend not only on academic credentials, but also on whether civilization develops effective bridges between human learning, meaningful contribution, and dignified life transitions. The essay suggests that education, employers, governments, and technological systems may need to share responsibility for maintaining these pathways. Scope and Limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an empirically established prediction. It does not claim that academic degrees will necessarily lose their value, that artificial intelligence will inevitably eliminate entry-level employment, or that one institutional model will suit every society. The possibilities discussed may emerge differently across countries, economic sectors, and social groups. The purpose is to contribute to public reflection and interdisciplinary research on education, artificial intelligence, employment transitions, institutional design, and human-centered civilization. items.title: Knowing When to Hand Over: A Survey of Uncertainty, Deferral, and Escalation in Human–AI Fraud Investigation
items.abstract: Language-model agents are being proposed to investigate fraud and money-laundering alerts under selective autonomy: the agent closes some cases itself and escalates the rest to a human analyst. Which cases it escalates determines the division of labor, the analysts' workload, and the errors that reach customers and regulators, yet the knowledge needed to design that rule is divided among learning to defer and selective prediction, uncertainty estimation for language models, and research on human reliance on AI advice. This survey connects the three through the escalation loop of a fraud-investigation team and restates known results from these literatures in one notation. We state the cost-optimal escalation rule, which requires different confidence thresholds for closing a case as benign and for concluding fraud, and its form under a fixed analyst capacity; show that calibration suffices for selective risk to be monotone and interpretable; state the conformal bound on the rate of cases that are both closed automatically and wrong; show when combining uncertainty signals helps and when correlated signals double-count; show that the error among automatically closed cases is not identified without audits and is estimable with them; and quantify how analyst reliance on the agent's verdict erodes the value of escalation. Against this basis we compare deferral rules and uncertainty signals, and conclude that threshold-based deferral rules assume a calibrated confidence that agents do not yet provide, that agent-level uncertainty estimation is only beginning, and that, to our knowledge, no peer-reviewed study has yet evaluated an escalation rule for a fraud-investigation agent together with the analysts who receive its cases.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Knowledge as Code
items.abstract: For millennia, knowledge has been carried by language, and large language models still put language at the center. Yet the coding agents built on these models mostly write code. This paper is a contribution to epistemology, which asks what kind of knowledge code is and how it is obtained. We define knowledge as code as knowledge written in a programming language or in a machine-parsable data format, whose validity can be checked by executing it. We define thirteen epistemic properties of knowledge media and show that code is the first medium to have all of them. We distinguish two ways in which knowledge enters code, encoding and learning by execution, where code is both the experiment and the record of its result. Agents make learning by execution observable, since their trajectories record every probe, observation and line of code they keep. Code is thus not only a tool of knowledge work but a knowledge medium in its own right, the first that can check what it holds.

items.title: La inteligencia artificial y sus implicaciones antihumanistas. Consecuencias de la delegación de la responsabilidad del pensar en las máquinas
items.abstract: Various voices warn of the growing anti-humanism that prevails today. This risk of the devaluation of humanity finds a salient example—in the context of posthumanism in its cybernetic form—in the unstoppable development of AI with the emergence of products such as ChatGPT, capable of generating literary, musical, or pictorial compositions. This is a technology that enables humans to delegate to non-thinking machines the responsibility for the task of thinking in its different domains—cognitive, evaluative, or artistic creation— thus running the risk of falling back, in Kantian terms, into a condition of immaturity. The task of thought—and, therefore, of philosophy—should consist in remaining vigilant in order to resist such temptations and, if possible, in exercising with greater firmness that faculty of thinking characteristic of humans, by analyzing the age in which they find themselves and the dangers that lie in wait for them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Labor markets and inequality
items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) changes labor markets and the distribution of income. It begins by distinguishing skill-biased, routine-biased, and task-biased technological change, then explains why generative AI requires a further shift in emphasis from occupations to tasks, workflows, and organizational control. The chapter argues that AI affects inequality through several channels at once: direct task displacement, productivity gains, the creation of new tasks, changes in market power, and differences in worker bargaining power. A central claim is that exposure to AI is not the same as technological unemployment. The distributional consequences depend on adoption costs, complementary investments, institutions, and the allocation of productivity rents inside firms and across markets. This chapter, therefore, treats AI neither as an automatic engine of mass unemployment nor as a neutral productivity tool, but as a general-purpose technology whose labor market effects are mediated by economic structure and policy.

items.title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
items.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

items.title: Large Language Model-Tuned Rule Distillation for Adversarial Ramp Cut-in Testing of Autonomous Vehicles
items.abstract: Highway ramp merging is a safety-critical interaction for automated-vehicle validation because gap acceptance, longitudinal control, and lane-changing responses are coupled within a short time horizon. This paper presents a rule-distillation framework in which a large language model (LLM) serves only as an offline calibrator of a compact, interpretable rule expert: the model receives scalar replay statistics and proposes bounded updates of three rule parameters, every candidate is verified by closed-loop simulation, and the accepted rule expert is re-executed under legal-action masking and safety filtering to produce feasible demonstrations for an adversarial ramp actor, which is then fine-tuned by multi-agent reinforcement learning on a fixed scenario-replay library. On the training-distribution library, the distilled adversary reaches the highest evaluation return and reward-collision rate of the three schemes. This advantage only partly carries over to 150 held-out scenarios, where its reward-collision rate becomes indistinguishable from that of training from scratch (42.7% against 40.7%, overlapping intervals) while its evaluation return and its rate of successfully induced evasive responses remain higher. Against random-search and Bayesian-optimization calibrators evaluated under the same parameter ranges, score and simulation budget, the LLM attains a comparable calibration score with roughly one third of the closed-loop simulations and with a smaller run-to-run spread, but it is not a better global optimizer at the full budget, so it is best characterized as a sample-efficient and low-variance calibrator. The results indicate that verified rule calibration provides effective initialization for adversarial reinforcement learning within the evaluated simulation setting.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of AI anxiety among medical imaging students: a cross-sectional study based on emotional flexibility and future employment anxiety
items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI anxiety among medical imaging students and to examine the associations of emotional flexibility, future employment anxiety, and demographic variables with profile membership, thereby providing empirical evidence for differentiated psychological intervention strategies. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted using convenience sampling among 488 medical imaging students recruited from North Sichuan Medical College in Sichuan Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale, the Emotional Flexibility Scale, the Future Employment Anxiety Scale, and a demographic questionnaire. Latent profile analysis was used to identify AI anxiety profiles, and the three-step BCH and R3STEP procedures were used to examine distal outcomes and covariates while accounting for classification uncertainty. Results Latent profile analysis identified three severity-ordered AI anxiety profiles: a Medium AI anxiety profile (65.78%), a High AI anxiety profile (22.75%), and a Low AI anxiety profile (11.48%). The High profile scored most prominently on Job Replacement and Sociotechnical Blindness anxiety. Emotional flexibility showed a nonlinear distribution across profiles: highest in the Low profile (BCH M = 3.975), lowest in the Medium profile (3.282), and intermediate in the High profile (3.805). Future employment anxiety increased monotonically across the profiles (Low: 2.285; Medium: 3.255; High: 4.126; all pairwise p < 0.001) and independently distinguished all profiles in the classification-error-adjusted (R3STEP) analysis. Emotional flexibility was lowest in the Medium profile and did not differ between the High and Low profiles ( p = 0.271); in the classification-error-adjusted analysis, it distinguished the High from the Medium profile but not the Low from the Medium profile. Conclusion The findings support differentiated psychological support tailored to distinct AI anxiety profiles, and suggest that AI literacy education and career planning guidance should be systematically integrated into medical imaging curricula.

items.title: Leadership in Neurodiverse AI-Augmented Organizations
items.abstract: Leadership in Neurodiverse, AI-Augmented Organizations explores the evolving nature of leadership in an era where artificial intelligence and human diversity are reshaping the future of work. As organizations increasingly adopt AI-powered technologies and embrace inclusive workplace practices, leaders are challenged to cultivate environments that value diverse cognitive abilities, foster innovation, and ensure ethical, people-centered decision-making. This edited volume brings together scholarly research, conceptual insights, empirical studies, and practical case analyses that examine how leadership can successfully integrate AI capabilities while empowering neurodiverse talent. It highlights the importance of adaptive leadership, emotional intelligence, digital transformation, inclusive organizational cultures, and responsible AI governance in building resilient and high-performing organizations.

items.title: Learn to Modify: Self-evolving Multi-agent Refinement Framework for Conversational Text-to-Motion Generation
items.abstract: Despite rapid progress in text-to-motion generation, existing methods are commonly designed for single-shot generation. When users are dissatisfied with specific motion details, they are often forced to regenerate the entire sequence from scratch, which is computationally inefficient and potentially destroys previously established kinematic context. A practical generation system should instead support iterative user feedback and refine only the affected spatio-temporal regions while preserving the remaining motion. Therefore, we introduce a conversational motion generation paradigm that requires the system to coordinate instruction understanding, motion generation, localized editing, and quality assessment. Recent advances in LLM-driven multi-agent systems provide a promising foundation for such role-specialized coordination. To tackle these challenges, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent RefinemenT Framework (SMART) is proposed for conversational motion generation. Within SMART, to preserve semantic consistency, we design a semantic-guided masked motion editing mechanism, which precisely grounds natural language feedback into spatiotemporal motion regions to enable localized refinements without altering unedited regions. To reduce redundant exploration, we propose a memory-based self-evolving strategy that dynamically accumulates motion editing knowledge from interaction history and reuses past successful experience. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SMART effectively supports multi-turn conversational motion generation and enables efficient motion refinement.

items.title: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.

items.title: Learning Out of Hours: A Narrative Review of Balancing Responsibility, Supervision, and Fatigue in Junior Doctor Training
items.abstract: Out-of-hours work is an integral component of postgraduate medical training and exposes junior doctors to clinical responsibility, uncertainty, competing demands, and acute deterioration in circumstances that may differ substantially from routine daytime practice. These conditions can provide valuable opportunities for experiential learning, but they can also reduce educational value when responsibility is accompanied by inadequate supervision, excessive workload or fatigue. This narrative review examines out-of-hours work as a learning environment for junior doctors, integrating literature on workplace learning, autonomy and supervision, prioritisation and decision-making, deterioration and escalation, handover and teamwork, sleep disruption and fatigue, and educational interventions designed to prepare trainees for out-of-hours practice. The literature suggests that the educational value of out-of-hours work arises not from independence alone, but from meaningful clinical responsibility within an appropriately supported environment. Responsibility can provide opportunities for autonomous initial assessment, prioritisation, and decision-making under uncertainty, while the recognition of personal limits and appropriate escalation are themselves components of developing clinical judgement. Simulation and structured preparation may help trainees rehearse these demands before substantial clinical responsibility is assumed, while feedback, reflection, and review of subsequent patient outcomes can help convert clinical exposure into learning. However, excessive workload, inadequate supervision, and fatigue may impair both the opportunity and the capacity to learn. Out-of-hours training should therefore aim to preserve authentic responsibility while ensuring that autonomy is graded to capability, senior support remains accessible, workload is manageable, and opportunities for feedback and recovery are maintained. We propose that effective out-of-hours learning occurs within a zone of meaningful responsibility in which trainees are sufficiently challenged to develop clinical judgement without becoming unsupported or physiologically unsustainable. Designing this environment requires attention not only to individual preparedness but also to supervision, staffing, workload, handover, feedback, and rota design.

items.title: Leveraging AI for Higher Education Human Resources:A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Human Resource Development (HRD) policies for academic staff in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) is often constrained by the misalignment between computational capabilities and institutional governance. While HEIs generate substantial datasets through the Tri Dharma (the three pillars of higher education: teaching, research, and community service), this data remains underutilized for proactive policy-making. To map the state-of-the-art and identify existing research gaps, this study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis of 400 unique peer-reviewed documents, obtained from an initial 485 records retrieved from Scopus (n = 260) and Web of Science (n = 225) after removing 85 duplicates, covering the seven-year period from 2018 to 2024. Visual analysis using VOSviewer reveals a distinct semantic-policy discrepancy, showing that semantic technologies and predictive AI models are researched as isolated technical domains, seldom integrated into comprehensive institutional governance. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development. The proposed framework integrates machine learning classifiers (Naïve Bayes, K-Means, and Apriori association) with a semantic Knowledge Graph layer to transform descriptive academic metrics into explainable, policy-conforming recommendations. Preliminary expert consultation with LLDIKTI Region II highlights the conceptual viability of the Framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development in mitigating administrative bottlenecks, supporting objective career path design, and minimizing human subjectivity in lecturer performance evaluations.

items.title: LLM agents in online communities draw fewer replies and more disagreement when labeled as AI
items.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.

items.title: Lo transido: límite ontológico de la inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: Thinking of the anguished as the ontological limit of artificial intelligence (AI) implies shifting the discussion from techniques to the mode of being. In the cybernetic discourse on AI, the logic of progressive overcoming predominates: more data, more speed, more simulation capacity. However, this logic presupposes that the difference between human and AI is quantitative, when in reality it is ontological. The anguished names precisely that which cannot be increased or optimized, because it is a condition of existence and entails physical and moral pain, as well as a dejection that traverses the human being. The anguished in the human is traversed by the world and the cyberworld as a planetary hybrid. It involves registering stimuli and processing information and being affected in one own being by what happens. Pain is a bodily fact and an experience that wounds, that marks, that leaves a trace on subjects, who are biological, psychological, and social entities; Time is an ordered sequence of moments and an experience of finitude, of waiting, of loss, and of anticipating death. Humanity knows this planetary hybrid and is exposed, compromised, and vulnerable to it. AI, on the other hand, can model pain, recognize its signs, and describe it with increasing precision, but it cannot suffer it. It can calculate time, anticipate future scenarios, and optimize decisions, but it does not experience time as finitude or angst.

items.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.

items.title: Local Faces of Global Employment Practices: Media Discourses on Uberization of Labor and Institutional Adaptation
items.abstract: Uberization has become a paradigmatic case of how platform-mediated work arrangements disrupt labour markets and existing institutional structures, yet we know little about the discursive processes through which such models are reworked within divergent capitalist systems. This article investigates how Uber’s employment model is received, contested and reshaped in the United Kingdom, Germany and Mexico. Linking translation theory and Varieties of Capitalism within a discursive legitimation perspective, we examine how global platform employment practices are received, contested, and evaluated across national institutional contexts. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of 3,771 newspaper articles (2012–2023) from the three countries, combining sentiment classification with thematic analysis. We identify discursive waves of (de)legitimation around Uber’s labour practices in distinct institutional constellations. The analysis reveals three trajectories: reactive accommodation under competitive and consumer pressures in the United Kingdom as a liberal market economy; proactive regulatory resistance rooted in labour institutions in Germany as a coordinated market economy; and delayed but intense contestation in Mexico as an emerging market economy characterized by hybrid, fragmented and highly informal arrangements. The study extends the discursive legitimation perspective by linking institutional theory and industrial relations theory to show how institutionally conditioned media discourses shape the (de)legitimation of global employment practices, while bringing emerging markets and informality more centrally into Varieties of Capitalism debates.

items.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
items.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

items.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

items.title: Los riesgos de la IA dialógica en la educación superior: afectaciones cognitivas y en la capacidad de lecto-escritura
items.abstract: Dialogic Artificial Intelligence (DAI) or communicative AI within Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly expanding across higher education and academic workflows in both teaching and research. The adoption of DAI is being driven by the pressure to enhance productivity and automate academic practices. This paper discusses the primary risks that the intensive use of DAI poses to human cognitive capacities, information biases, and the erosion of literacy, critical thinking, argumentation, and academic discourse skills. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging forms of plagiarism and misconduct facilitated by DAI while reflecting on the concept of individual authorship, which has become obsolete, giving way to human-AI co-authorship. As an immersive technology that impacts human agency and autonomy, DAI could irreversibly transform cognition, literacy, the sense of authorship, and collaborative frameworks in research, teaching, and scholarly production. Finally, it concludes with a set of criteria and recommendations to guide university regulatory policies on DAI, moving beyond prohibitions, punitive measures, or ineffective appeals to individual ethics in the use of LLMs.

items.title: Mammography datasets and artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection: challenges, bias, and future directions
items.abstract: Background Breast cancer is still one of the main causes of death in women from cancer worldwide, and early detection is crucial. Mammography is the primary imaging modality for breast cancer screening and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced automated breast cancer detection. This review takes a data-centered approach, examining key characteristics of public datasets, the contributions of mammography data to AI for breast cancer detection, and the implications for clinical generalizability. This review, however, takes a data-centered approach, critically analyzing characteristics of publicly available mammography datasets, and the role of mammography data to the development, performance and clinical generalization of AI models for the detection of breast cancer. The datasets are compared on the following aspects: dataset size, quality of the annotations, imaging modality, clinical metadata, dataset accessibility and demographic diversity. Analysis reveals that the quality, diversity and representativeness of the data used are critical for the performance and generalizability of AI models, ranging from the traditional machine learning era to the current era of deep learning, transformer-based systems, multimodal learning, explainable AI and privacy-preserving learning. Conclusion The results show that, apart from the development of AI model architectures, it is a necessity to have standardized, diverse and clinically representative datasets to make further progress in AI-assisted mammography. The review emphasizes the importance of establishing a comprehensive benchmark dataset for mammography that is large and diverse to enhance reproducibility, to fairly evaluate models, and to develop strong, clinically viable AI systems for breast cancer detection.

items.title: Manifold-Informed Neural Networks for Low-Label ECG Electrolyte Inference
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_ϕ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_ϕ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

items.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

items.title: Measuring the spread of trust and distrust through influence in human-autonomy teams
items.abstract: Trust in human-autonomy teams is dynamic and shaped by ongoing interaction, yet most measures rely on retrospective self-report, limiting detection of how trust and distrust propagate in real time. This study introduces and validates influence-an interaction-based metric computed as the average mutual information between joint and team-state time series-to track the spread of trust and distrust. Forty-five participants completed five simulated Remotely Piloted Aircraft System missions in three-member teams, with trust manipulated through communicative and behavioural spreading across congruent, mismatched, and human-versus-agent conditions. Influence predicted subjective team trust and objective performance during active spreading but not in a no-spreading control and showed strong reliability and construct validity. As validation checks, influence recovered known effects: credibility violations damaged trust most, and human sources outweighed agents. Critically, the influence-trust relationship reversed direction across contexts, revealing a context-dependent mechanism. Influence thus offers a real-time, unobtrusive measure linking interaction structure to team outcomes.

items.abstract: Translating preclinical findings into safe and effective pharmacotherapy for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains a major challenge in pediatric neuropsychopharmacology.This review critically examines why some mechanism-based therapies translate successfully from animal models to clinical practice, whereas others fail despite promising preclinical evidence.Among available models, the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) exhibits strong construct validity and domain-specific predictive validity for conserved catecholaminergic mechanisms relevant to ADHD.Across species, successful therapies generally preserve mechanistic continuity by enhancing prefrontal catecholamine signaling through dopamine transporter inhibition, norepinephrine transporter blockade, or 2A-adrenergic receptor stimulation.Accordingly, stimulants, atomoxetine, guanfacine, and viloxazine extended-release show substantial translational and clinical success.Pediatric trials support this hierarchy, with clinician-rated standardized mean differences versus placebo of approximately 1.02 for amphetamines, 0.78 for methylphenidate, and 0.56 for atomoxetine at around 12 weeks.In contrast, nicotinic and histaminergic agents and certain dopaminergic antagonist strategies have translated poorly because of inadequate target engagement, developmental pharmacokinetic differences, and pediatric safety concerns.Importantly, SHR predictive validity is domain-specific rather than syndrome-wide, as methylphenidate more consistently improves attention and impulsivity than locomotor hyperactivity.Precision medicine, pharmacogenomics, biomarker-guided target engagement, and artificial intelligence-assisted approaches may improve future drug development.Overall, current evidence supports mechanistic continuity, rather than broad behavioral similarity, as a useful framework for translating preclinical findings into effective pediatric ADHD therapies, although prospective evaluation and refinement of this framework remain necessary.
